The urgent testing plan — prioritizing FVIII assay after aPTT/mixing study — reflects standard diagnostic hierarchy for suspected hemophilia. Critically, no new contradictory data (e.g., inhibitor confirmed, normal FVIII, or autosomal family pattern) has emerged; thus, hemophilia A remains the single most likely diagnosis.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Atraumatic hemarthrosis is the most common initial presentation of previously undiagnosed hemophilia A.  
- Maternal uncle affected — classic X-linked recessive transmission pattern (carrier mother → 50% risk to male offspring).  
- Isolated intrinsic pathway abnormality (prolonged ACT, normal PT/platelets) — matches FVIII deficiency biochemistry.  
- Diagnostic workflow explicitly prioritizes Factor VIII activity assay as the definitive test — indicating clinical alignment with hemophilia A.  
- Hemophilia A is 5–6× more prevalent than hemophilia B and vastly more common than type 3 VWD.  
- Absence of mucosal/surgical bleeding history makes FXI deficiency unlikely, as it does not typically present with spontaneous joint bleeds.

[GAPS]  
- Actual aPTT value and mixing study result — still pending; required to confirm factor deficiency (vs. inhibitor) before interpreting FVIII level.  
- Quantitative Factor VIII activity — not yet reported; essential to confirm diagnosis and classify severity (mild/moderate/severe).  
- Factor IX activity — needed to definitively exclude hemophilia B.  
- VWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity — required to rule out type 2N or 3 VWD if FVIII is low but discordant with VWF levels.  
- Genetic testing (F8 gene sequencing) — not yet performed; gold standard for confirmation and carrier testing in family.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)
